quote: The review PICO (planned at the protocol stage) is the PICO on which eligibility of studies is based
The PICO for each synthesis (also planned at the protocol stage) defines the question that each specific synthesis aims to answer
The PICO of the included studies (determined at the review stage) is what was actually investigated in the included studies.
Equal emphasis in addressing, and equal precision in defining, each PICO component is not necessary.
It is generally not possible to formulate an answerable question for a review without knowing some of the studies relevant to the question
JBI suggests utilising the PCC (population, concept and context) approach to formulate review questions for scoping reviews.
A scoping review question is broader than those in systematic reviews and can be seen as hypothesis-generating, whereas a systematic review is hypothesis-testing
there may be a compelling argument to use a different question format (such as PICO or Population, Exposure, Comparator, Outcome [PECO])
If a review question is unclear, the review will lack coherence.
each element of the PCC approach is broken down into a further description of what the review will include and exclude.
If changes are made, deviations from the protocol with supporting justification should be made transparent within the final scoping review
Crossmark lets readers know when a substantial change affecting the citation or interpretation has occurred
Members place the Crossmark button close to the title of an item on their web pages and in PDFs.
